entities.name: Mahabodhi Temple
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Mahabodhi Temple in Bodh Gaya, Bihar, India marks the site where Siddhartha Gautama attained enlightenment under a Bodhi tree to become the Buddha — the most sacred site in Buddhism. The temple complex, designated a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2002, has drawn Buddhist pilgrims from across Asia for 2,500 years, and the sacred Bodhi tree standing beside the temple is a direct descendant of the original tree under which the Buddha sat.

Emperor Ashoka of the Maurya Empire visited Bodh Gaya around 260 BCE after his conversion to Buddhism and built the first temple structure and diamond throne marking the enlightenment spot. The current temple was built in the 5th-6th centuries CE, though it has undergone multiple restorations including a major 19th-century renovation funded by the King of Burma (1880-1884). The inner sanctum houses a large gilded image of the Buddha seated in the enlightenment pose (bhumisparsha mudra).

The Bodhi tree (Ficus religiosa) stands northwest of the temple: the original tree died, but a sapling was brought to Sri Lanka in the 3rd century BCE (the Jaya Sri Maha Bodhi, which still lives), and a branch was returned to Bodh Gaya. The site's sacredness makes it the destination of Buddhist pilgrims from Thailand, Japan, Sri Lanka, China, Korea, and Myanmar, creating a unique convergence of Asian Buddhist traditions at a single historical site.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Mahabodhi Temple marks the site of Buddhism's founding moment — the Buddha's enlightenment — making Bodh Gaya the most sacred pilgrimage destination in one of the world's major religions, with 500 million adherents.
